items.stem: A company hosts a web application on Amazon EC2 instances. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and the target group checks the health of the application on each instance. The Auto Scaling group uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks. Sometimes the application on an instance stops answering HTTP requests, but the instance keeps running. The company must ensure that failed instances are replaced automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks
stops answering HTTP requests, but the instance keeps running

options.text: Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group, so that the group also acts on the results of the target group health checks.
options.why: For an instance that fails the target group check, [Elastic Load Balancing stops sending traffic to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace), and the group [replaces it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-unhealthy-replaced), with one setting and no code.

options.text: Keep the current health check settings of the Auto Scaling group, and let the group replace the instances that its health checks find unhealthy.
options.why: By default the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks, and the running instance passes its EC2 status checks, so it stays in service.

options.text: Run a script on each instance that tests the application every minute and calls the Auto Scaling API to mark the instance unhealthy when a test fails.
options.why: It works, because a custom check can [mark that particular instance as](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-custom-health-check-immediate-replace) unhealthy, but the team writes code that one setting replaces.

options.text: Increase the health check grace period of the Auto Scaling group, so that the group waits longer before it checks the health of each new instance.
options.why: The grace period is the [minimum amount of time (in seconds)](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-grace-period-definition) before the group can terminate a new instance for failed health; it adds no load balancer check.
options.misconception: believes the grace period decides which health checks the group uses

items.explanation: The application fails while the instance keeps running, so the EC2 status checks still pass. By default the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks. For the ELB health check type, [you must turn it on](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-check-must-be-turned-on); then the group marks the instance unhealthy [on its next periodic health check](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-unhealthy-replaced).
items.takeaway: A running instance with a failed application needs the ELB health check type on the group.
items.twin: If the stem said "the underlying hardware of an instance fails, and the instance fails its EC2 system status check" instead: keep the current settings, because EC2 status checks are the [default health check type](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-check-type-ec2-default).
items.say: The group ignores the load balancer checks until you turn them on, so I'd set the health check type to ELB.

solvers.stem_only: The application fails while the instance stays running, so EC2 status checks never see it. Add the ELB health check type to the Auto Scaling group so it replaces instances that the target group marks unhealthy.

items.stem: A company runs a stateless web application on one Amazon EC2 instance. During the day the load changes often, and at peaks the CPU utilization of the instance reaches 100%. Users then see slow responses. The company expects the number of users to grow during the next year. The application must handle the growth and the daily peaks with minimal downtime. Which solution will meet these requirements?
keywords: stateless web application on one Amazon EC2 instance

options.text: Change the instance to a larger instance type with more vCPUs and more memory, and move to a larger type again each time the load grows.
options.why: To change the type, [you must stop your instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required), so each resize brings downtime, and one instance still serves all users from one place.

options.text: Turn on detailed monitoring for the instance, so that Amazon CloudWatch publishes the CPU utilization metric every minute instead of every five minutes.
options.why: Detailed monitoring reports the metric more often, but it adds no instance, so the single instance still runs out of CPU at the peaks.
options.misconception: believes that more frequent metrics add capacity

options.text: Run the application in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer, with a target tracking scaling policy on CPU utilization.
options.why: Adding instances is [essential for dynamic workloads with fluctuating demands](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-decision-guide-horizontal-for-fluctuating), and target tracking [adjusts the number of EC2 instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-target-tracking-definition) while the other instances keep serving.

options.text: Attach a second elastic network interface to the instance, so that the instance can accept twice as many user requests during the peaks.
options.why: A second network interface adds a network path, not vCPUs, so the CPU utilization of the single instance still reaches 100% at the peaks.
options.misconception: believes that a second network interface adds compute capacity

items.explanation: The load changes during the day and grows over time. Horizontal scaling is [essential for dynamic workloads with fluctuating demands](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-decision-guide-horizontal-for-fluctuating), and stateless servers can be [replaced at will without causing an availability impact](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-stateless-servers-replaceable). A group behind a load balancer adds and removes instances while the others keep serving.
items.takeaway: For changing load on a stateless tier, scale out with an Auto Scaling group instead of scaling up.
items.twin: If the stem said "the application keeps its state in memory and cannot run as several copies" instead: a larger instance type with a planned stop, because [you must stop your instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required) to resize it.
items.say: It's stateless and the load moves, so I'd scale out with an Auto Scaling group instead of resizing one instance.

solvers.stem_only: Scale horizontally: put the stateless app in an Auto Scaling group across at least two AZs behind an ALB with a target tracking policy on CPU.

items.stem: A company runs long-running video jobs on On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group. Each worker instance takes one job from an Amazon SQS queue, and a job can run for up to 2 hours. The number of jobs changes during the day, and the group scales in when the queue is short. Scale in must not stop a running job. Operators sometimes terminate worker instances by mistake in the Amazon EC2 console, and the company must ensure that this cannot happen. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: Scale in must not stop a running job
terminate worker instances by mistake in the Amazon EC2 console

options.text: Turn on instance scale-in protection for every worker instance at all times, so that neither scale in nor the EC2 console can terminate a worker.
options.why: Scale-in protection does not block a manual termination, and kept on all day it blocks every scale in. For manual termination, AWS says to [enable Amazon EC2 termination protection](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scale-in-protection-ec2-termination-protection-for-manual).

options.text: Have each worker turn on instance scale-in protection for its own instance when a job starts, and turn the protection off when the job ends.
options.why: AWS suggests that you [use instance scale-in protection](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-unprocessed-messages-return) for long-running workers; with the protection off after each job, the group can remove idle workers.

options.text: Suspend the Terminate process of the Auto Scaling group, so that the group does not terminate any worker instance when it scales in.
options.why: It protects running jobs, but it gives you [complete control over all EC2 instance terminations](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-suspend-terminate-full-control), so idle workers keep running and the company pays for them.

options.text: Turn on Amazon EC2 termination protection for each worker instance that the group launches, so that a termination request from the EC2 console fails.
options.why: Scale-in protection does not cover the console. [To protect Auto Scaling instances from manual termination](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scale-in-protection-ec2-termination-protection-for-manual), you [enable Amazon EC2 termination protection](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scale-in-protection-ec2-termination-protection-for-manual).

options.text: Move the workers to Spot Instances, and add a termination lifecycle hook that keeps each Spot Instance running until its current job ends.
options.why: A lifecycle hook [does not prevent an instance from terminating](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-spot-two-minute-notice) when Amazon EC2 reclaims Spot capacity, so a long job can stop after a [two-minute interruption notice](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-spot-two-minute-notice).

items.explanation: Scale in and manual termination are two different paths. For scale in, AWS says to [use instance protection to prevent](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-termination-policy-and-instance-protection) the group from choosing specific instances, and a worker that sets it per job keeps idle workers removable. For the console, you [enable Amazon EC2 termination protection](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scale-in-protection-ec2-termination-protection-for-manual).
items.takeaway: Scale-in protection guards against scale in; EC2 termination protection guards against manual termination.
items.twin: If the stem said "the workers run on Spot Instances" instead: plan for interruptions, because Spot interruptions [bypass all Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling protection mechanisms](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-interruption-bypasses-all-protection).
items.say: Scale-in protection per job stops the group, and EC2 termination protection stops a person in the console.

solvers.stem_only: Workers set instance scale-in protection on themselves while a job runs and clear it after (stops scale in from killing jobs); scale-in protection does not block manual terminations, so also enable EC2 termination protection (DisableApiTermination) to stop console terminations.

items.stem: A company runs a batch application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The group was created several years ago from a launch configuration, and it uses one instance type. To lower cost, the company now wants the group to run Spot Instances above a base of On-Demand Instances, and to use several instance types. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: created several years ago from a launch configuration
Spot Instances above a base of On-Demand Instances

options.text: Edit the existing launch configuration to add a Spot purchase option and the extra instance types, and keep the group attached to it.
options.why: You [can't modify a launch configuration](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-config-immutable), and a launch configuration cannot create a group that [launches both Spot and On-Demand Instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-config-no-mixed-types).

options.text: Create a second launch configuration for the Spot Instances, and attach it to the group next to the current launch configuration.
options.why: A group can [only specify one launch configuration](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-launch-configuration-one-and-immutable) at a time, so a second one cannot be attached.
options.misconception: believes that a group can use one launch configuration per purchase option

options.text: Keep the group for the On-Demand base, and create a separate Spot Fleet with several instance types that the team scales with its own scripts.
options.why: It works, but the team runs and scales a second fleet with its own scripts, while one group with a launch template does the same job.

options.text: Create a launch template with the same settings, and update the group to use it with a mixed instances policy that lists the instance types.
options.why: Several purchase options are possible [only when you use a launch template](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-purchase-options-need-launch-template), and one group then holds the On-Demand base, the Spot capacity and the instance types.

items.explanation: A launch configuration cannot create a group that [launches both Spot and On-Demand Instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-config-no-mixed-types); for that you [must use a launch template](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-config-no-mixed-types). With a mixed instances policy, the group's [base capacity be fulfilled with On-Demand instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-on-demand-base-spot-above) can stay, and Spot Instances fill the capacity above it.
items.takeaway: Spot and On-Demand Instances, or several instance types, in one group need a launch template.
items.twin: If the stem said "the group already uses a launch template" instead: add a mixed instances policy to the group, because multiple purchase options work [only when you use a launch template](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-purchase-options-need-launch-template).
items.say: A launch configuration can't mix Spot and On-Demand, so I'd move the group to a launch template with a mixed instances policy.

solvers.stem_only: Launch configurations cannot do mixed instances or Spot plus On-Demand base; migrate to a launch template and use a mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base and several instance types.

items.stem: A company hosts a web application on Amazon EC2 instances. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and the target group checks the health of the application on each instance. The Auto Scaling group uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks. Sometimes the underlying hardware of an instance fails, and the instance fails its EC2 system status check. The company must ensure that failed instances are replaced automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: uses only the default Amazon EC2 health checks
fails its EC2 system status check

options.text: Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group, so that the group also acts on the results of the target group health checks.
options.why: It works, but it is a change that this failure does not need, because the EC2 status checks of the group already catch impaired hardware.

options.text: Keep the current health check settings of the Auto Scaling group, and let the group replace the instances that its health checks find unhealthy.
options.why: EC2 status checks are [always enabled](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-ec2-status-checks-always-enabled) for the group, and an instance whose [hardware has become impaired](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-unhealthy-instance-definition) counts as unhealthy and is replaced.

options.text: Run a script on each instance that tests the application every minute and calls the Auto Scaling API to mark the instance unhealthy when a test fails.
options.why: It adds code to maintain, and a script on failed hardware stops with the hardware; the default EC2 checks already find this failure.

options.text: Increase the health check grace period of the Auto Scaling group, so that the group waits longer before it checks the health of each new instance.
options.why: The grace period is the [minimum amount of time (in seconds)](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-grace-period-definition) before the group can terminate a new instance for failed health; it changes no check.
options.misconception: believes the grace period decides which health checks the group uses

items.explanation: The hardware fails, so the instance fails its EC2 system status check. EC2 status checks are the [default health check type](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-check-type-ec2-default) of the group, and the group [automatically terminates it and replaces it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-replaces-impaired-instance). The current settings meet the requirement with no change and no work.
items.takeaway: Impaired hardware fails the EC2 status checks, and the group acts on those checks with its default settings.
items.twin: If the stem said "the target group marks the instance unhealthy, and the instance still passes its EC2 status checks" instead: turn on ELB health checks, because the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) checks by default.
items.say: The EC2 status checks are on in every group, so a hardware failure is already replaced; no change needed.

solvers.stem_only: A failed EC2 system status check is already detected by the default EC2 health checks of the group, which replaces the impaired instance. No change is needed.

items.stem: A company runs an analytics application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. When an instance starts, the application loads a large data set into memory, which takes about 15 minutes. Traffic rises several times a day at times that are hard to predict, and new instances serve users too late. The instance type supports hibernation. The company wants faster scale-out without paying for running instances that wait for traffic. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: loads a large data set into memory
without paying for running instances that wait

options.text: Hibernate the instances of the Auto Scaling group when traffic is low, and start them again from hibernation when traffic rises.
options.why: [You can't hibernate an instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-cannot-hibernate-group-instance) in an Auto Scaling group; the group [marks the stopped instance as unhealthy](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-cannot-hibernate-group-instance) and can replace it.

options.text: Add a warm pool to the Auto Scaling group, and keep the warm pool instances in the Hibernated state until the group needs them.
options.why: Hibernated warm pool instances [save the contents of your RAM](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pool-hibernated-ram), so the data set waits in memory, and you [pay only for the EBS volumes](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pool-hibernated-ram) and Elastic IP addresses.

options.text: Raise the minimum capacity of the Auto Scaling group to the number of instances that the highest traffic of the day needs.
options.why: It works, but the group then pays for peak capacity all day, because instances are billed [as soon as they are launched](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-billed-from-launch).

options.text: Change the launch template to a larger instance type, so that each new instance loads the data set faster and serves more users.
options.why: A larger instance type still loads the data set at each start, and to change the type of a running instance [you must stop your instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required).

items.explanation: A warm pool keeps a [pool of pre-initialized EC2 instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pool-definition) beside the group. In the Hibernated state, the instances [save the contents of your RAM](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pool-hibernated-ram), so the data set is in memory when an instance leaves the pool. No warm pool instance runs while it waits.
items.takeaway: Slow start at scale-out: a warm pool of Stopped or Hibernated instances, not hibernation inside the group.
items.twin: If the stem said "the application starts in a few seconds" instead: no warm pool, because a warm pool that the application does not need [can lead to unnecessary costs](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-warm-pool-unnecessary-cost).
items.say: I'd add a warm pool in the Hibernated state, so the memory is ready and only the volumes cost money.

solvers.stem_only: Use a warm pool with instances in the Hibernated state: memory (the loaded data set) is preserved and only storage is paid while waiting, so scale-out is fast and cheap.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The group has one simple scaling policy that adds two instances when average CPU utilization is above 70%, and the group uses the default cooldown. Traffic is spiky. When a second spike comes a few minutes after the first one, the group adds no instances until the cooldown ends. New instances also show high CPU utilization while they start, which once caused a scale-out that was not needed. Which change will solve both problems in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: adds no instances until the cooldown ends
high CPU utilization while they start

options.text: Keep the simple scaling policy, and lower the default cooldown of the group to 60 seconds, so that the policy can react to each new spike sooner.
options.why: A shorter cooldown lets the start-up load of new instances start even more scale-outs, and AWS advises: [do not use simple scaling policies](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-simple-scaling-not-recommended).
options.misconception: believes that a shorter cooldown fixes simple scaling without side effects

options.text: Replace the simple scaling policy with a target tracking scaling policy, and lower the default cooldown, because the new policy also waits for the cooldown.
options.why: Target tracking scales out [without waiting for the cooldown period to end](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-cooldown-target-tracking-step-do-not-wait), so a lower cooldown changes nothing, and without a warmup the start-up load still counts.

options.text: Replace the simple scaling policy with a target tracking scaling policy on average CPU utilization, and turn on a default instance warmup for the group.
options.why: Target tracking can scale out [without waiting for the cooldown period to end](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-cooldown-target-tracking-step-do-not-wait), and the warmup is the time a new instance [waits before contributing usage data](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-default-instance-warmup-purpose).

options.text: Keep the simple scaling policy, and raise the minimum capacity of the group to the number of instances that the largest spike needs.
options.why: It works for the spikes, but the group then pays for the capacity of the largest spike all day, also when traffic is low.

items.explanation: The cooldown applies to [scaling activities initiated by simple scaling policies](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-cooldown-applies-to-simple-scaling). Target tracking uses a warmup instead: a new instance is [not counted toward the aggregated EC2 instance metrics](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-warmup-instance-not-in-metrics) until its warmup ends. The new policy reacts to the second spike, and start-up load starts no extra scale-out.
items.takeaway: Cooldowns belong to simple scaling; target tracking and step scaling use an instance warmup.
items.twin: If the stem said "traffic rises at the same time every weekday" instead: also add a scheduled action before that time, because scheduled scaling fits when [the need arises on a predictable schedule](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use).
items.say: Swap simple scaling for target tracking and turn on instance warmup; the cooldown then stops getting in the way.

solvers.stem_only: Move to target tracking (no cooldown blocking repeated scale-out) and set a default instance warmup so metrics from starting instances are not counted.

items.stem: A company has an Auto Scaling group that runs On-Demand Instances of one instance type in two Availability Zones. The group uses the default termination policy. Availability Zone A has three instances: two were launched from the current version of the launch template, and one from an older version. Availability Zone B has two instances from the current version, and one of them is the oldest instance in the group. No instance has scale-in protection. The group now scales in by one instance. Which instance does the group terminate?
keywords: Availability Zone A has three instances
one of them is the oldest instance in the group

options.text: The instance in Availability Zone A that was launched from the older version of the launch template.
options.why: Zone A [has the most instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-default-zone-with-most), and the default policy is designed to [terminate instances that are using outdated configurations first](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-default-outdated-first).

options.text: The instance in Availability Zone B that is the oldest instance in the group, because it has run the longest.
options.why: The group [always balances instances across Availability Zones first](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-az-balance-first), and [OldestInstance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-policy-oldest-instance) is a policy that you choose, not the default.

options.text: The newest instance in Availability Zone A, because the group removes the most recent launch first.
options.why: To [terminate the newest instance in the group](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-policy-newest-instance) is the rule of the NewestInstance policy, which you choose; the default policy looks for outdated configurations.
options.misconception: confuses the default termination policy with the NewestInstance policy

options.text: One instance chosen at random from all five instances, because the default termination policy treats every zone the same.
options.why: The default policy first picks the zone that [has the most instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-default-zone-with-most), and a random choice comes last, among instances [closest to the next billing hour](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-default-billing-hour-then-random).
options.misconception: believes that the default termination policy ignores Availability Zones

items.explanation: First, the group picks the Availability Zone that [has the most instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-default-zone-with-most): Zone A, with three. Inside Zone A, the default policy is designed to [terminate instances that are using outdated configurations first](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-default-outdated-first). The instance from the older launch template version is the outdated one.
items.takeaway: On scale in, zone balance comes first; then the default policy removes outdated configurations.
items.twin: If the stem said "the group uses the OldestInstance termination policy" instead: the oldest instance of Zone A, because the group [always balances instances across Availability Zones first](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-az-balance-first).
items.say: Zone balance first, then outdated configuration, so the old-version instance in the bigger zone goes.

solvers.stem_only: Default termination policy first picks the AZ with the most instances (A, 3 vs 2), then the instance with the oldest launch template version, so the AZ A instance from the older version.

items.stem: A company runs an application on On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Each instance writes application logs to its local disk. The group scales in several times a day. The company must ensure that the logs of an instance are copied to Amazon S3 before the instance is terminated. The copy takes about 3 minutes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: writes application logs to its local disk
copied to Amazon S3 before the instance is terminated

options.text: Increase the deregistration delay of the target group to 10 minutes, so that each instance has time to copy its logs before termination.
options.why: The delay keeps existing connections open [until the deregistration delay expires](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-deregisters-on-scale-in); it runs no code, so nothing copies the logs.

options.text: Add a script to the user data of the launch template that copies the logs to Amazon S3 when the instance shuts down.
options.why: By default, user data scripts [run only during the boot cycle](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-user-data-runs-at-first-launch-by-default) of the first launch, not at shutdown.
options.misconception: believes that user data scripts run when an instance shuts down

options.text: Suspend the Terminate process of the group, and have an operator copy the logs of each instance to Amazon S3 before terminating it by hand.
options.why: It works, but operators copy logs and terminate instances by hand several times a day, which a lifecycle hook does without people.

options.text: Add a termination lifecycle hook to the group, and use the wait state to copy the logs to Amazon S3 before completing the lifecycle action.
options.why: On scale in, the hook [pauses the instance before it is terminated](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-scale-in-use), and in the wait state a script or a Lambda function can [download logs or other data](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-scale-in-use).

items.explanation: A termination lifecycle hook [extends the life of your Amazon EC2 instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-termination-hook-extends-life) after the group selects it for termination. A script or an AWS Lambda function copies the logs and then completes the lifecycle action. The default heartbeat timeout of [3600 seconds](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-heartbeat-timeout-default) leaves enough time for the copy.
items.takeaway: Save logs or finish work before scale in with a termination lifecycle hook.
items.twin: If the stem said "the instances are Spot Instances that Amazon EC2 reclaims" instead: copy the logs continuously, because a hook [does not prevent an instance from terminating](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-spot-two-minute-notice) when Spot capacity goes away.
items.say: I'd add a termination lifecycle hook: it pauses the instance, the logs go to S3, and then termination continues.

solvers.stem_only: Add a termination lifecycle hook; during Terminating:Wait copy the logs to S3, then complete the lifecycle action.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group with a target tracking scaling policy. Traffic follows the same daily pattern, with a peak every afternoon, and new instances need several minutes before they serve users. The group has 3 weeks of metric history. The operations team plans to create an AWS Auto Scaling scaling plan for the group, only to get predictive scaling. Which solution will add predictive scaling with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an AWS Auto Scaling scaling plan for the application, and turn on predictive scaling for the Auto Scaling group inside the plan.
options.why: It works, but AWS recommends predictive policies [directly on your Auto Scaling resources instead](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-plans-prefer-native-predictive-policies) of a plan used only for predictive scaling.

options.text: Add a predictive scaling policy directly to the Auto Scaling group, and keep the target tracking scaling policy that the group uses today.
options.why: Predictive scaling is a [native scaling policy in EC2 Auto Scaling](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-predictive-policy-vs-scaling-plan), so the group gets the forecast without a scaling plan, next to its target tracking policy.

options.text: Register the Auto Scaling group as a scalable target in Application Auto Scaling, and attach a predictive scaling policy to that target.
options.why: For EC2 instances, [use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-wa-ec2-auto-scaling-for-instances-application-auto-scaling-for-other-services); Application Auto Scaling is for other services, such as Amazon ECS.

options.text: Write an AWS Lambda function that reads the metric history each day and creates scheduled actions for the expected afternoon peak.
options.why: It can work for a fixed pattern, but the team writes and runs code that a predictive scaling policy replaces with one setting.

items.explanation: A predictive scaling policy is a [native scaling policy in EC2 Auto Scaling](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-predictive-policy-vs-scaling-plan), so the team does not have to [create an AWS Auto Scaling plan](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-predictive-policy-vs-scaling-plan) for it. The policy can [proactively increase capacity ahead of upcoming demand](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-predictive-ahead-of-demand), and the target tracking policy keeps following the load.
items.takeaway: Predictive scaling for an EC2 group is a policy of the group itself, without a scaling plan.
items.twin: If the stem said "the group has 6 hours of metric history" instead: keep target tracking for now, because predictive scaling needs [at least 24 hours of data](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-needs-24-hours-of-data).
items.say: Add a predictive scaling policy straight to the group; a scaling plan only adds work.

solvers.stem_only: No scaling plan needed: add a predictive scaling policy directly to the Auto Scaling group and keep the target tracking policy for real-time changes.

items.stem: A company runs image-processing workers on Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group. The jobs can tolerate interruption, because an unfinished job returns to the queue. When Amazon EC2 reclaims Spot capacity, the group loses several workers at once, and the replacements start only after the old instances are gone. The backlog then grows for several minutes. The company wants to keep Spot pricing. Which change will make the worker group MOST resilient to Spot interruptions?
keywords: the replacements start only after the old instances are gone

options.text: Add a termination lifecycle hook to the group, so that Amazon EC2 waits until each worker finishes its current job before it reclaims the instance.
options.why: A lifecycle hook [does not prevent an instance from terminating](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-spot-two-minute-notice) when Spot capacity is reclaimed; the worker gets a [two-minute interruption notice](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-spot-two-minute-notice).

options.text: Turn on instance scale-in protection for every worker instance, so that Amazon EC2 does not reclaim a worker while it processes a job.
options.why: Spot interruptions [bypass all Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling protection mechanisms](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-interruption-bypasses-all-protection), scale-in protection included.

options.text: Turn on Capacity Rebalancing for the Auto Scaling group, so that the group launches a new Spot Instance when a running one is at risk.
options.why: The group launches a replacement when an instance is [at an elevated risk of interruption](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-capacity-rebalancing-spot), and [then terminates an earlier instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-capacity-rebalancing-spot).

options.text: Change the Spot allocation strategy of the group to lowest-price, so that the group launches its workers from the cheapest Spot pools.
options.why: It keeps Spot pricing, but the lowest-price strategy has the [highest risk of interruption](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-lowest-price-not-recommended), so more workers stop.
options.misconception: believes that the cheapest Spot pools are as stable as the others

items.explanation: Without Capacity Rebalancing, the group waits [until after the Amazon EC2 Spot service interrupts](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-no-capacity-rebalancing-replace-after-interruption) an instance before it replaces it. With Capacity Rebalancing, the group starts a replacement when an instance is [at an elevated risk of interruption](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-capacity-rebalancing-spot), while the old worker still runs.
items.takeaway: To replace Spot workers before they are interrupted, turn on Capacity Rebalancing.
items.twin: If the stem said "the workers keep state that cannot be lost" instead: On-Demand Instances, because Amazon EC2 [can interrupt and reclaim your instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-interruption-bypasses-all-protection) in a Spot group.
items.say: Turn on Capacity Rebalancing, so the group starts a new Spot worker when the old one is at risk.

solvers.stem_only: Turn on Capacity Rebalancing so the group launches replacement Spot Instances when it gets a rebalance recommendation, before the at-risk instances are reclaimed (ideally with diversified pools / price-capacity-optimized).

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon ECS. The application stores orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table that uses provisioned capacity mode. During sales events, the number of requests grows quickly and then falls again. The company wants the number of ECS tasks and the read and write capacity of the table to follow the load automatically. Which AWS service should a solutions architect use to scale both resources?
keywords: read and write capacity of the table

options.text: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, with an Auto Scaling group whose scaling policy adds ECS tasks and DynamoDB table capacity
options.why: EC2 Auto Scaling is the choice when you [only need to scale Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-use-ec2-vs-aws-auto-scaling) groups; tasks and table capacity are not instances in a group.

options.text: Application Auto Scaling, with a target tracking scaling policy for the ECS service and another one for the DynamoDB table
options.why: Application Auto Scaling scales resources other than EC2 instances, and it supports [target tracking scaling](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-aas-policy-types) for the ECS service and for the table.

options.text: Elastic Load Balancing, with an Application Load Balancer that spreads the growing number of requests across the ECS tasks
options.why: A load balancer [automatically distributes your incoming traffic](../facts/elb.md#elb-what-distributes-traffic-across-targets) across targets, but it adds no tasks and no table capacity.
options.misconception: believes that spreading requests adds capacity

options.text: Amazon CloudFront, with a distribution that caches the responses of the ECS tasks so that fewer requests reach the table
options.why: A cache in front of the tasks changes neither the number of ECS tasks nor the read and write capacity of the table.
options.misconception: believes that a cache in front of an application scales its resources

items.explanation: An ECS service and a DynamoDB table are not EC2 instances. For resources like these, [you can use the Application Auto Scaling API](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-faq-application-auto-scaling-for-non-ec2). An ECS service supports [auto scaling of its task count](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-aas-scalable-dimension-examples), and a table in provisioned mode scales [the read and write capacity of the table](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-aas-scalable-dimension-examples).
items.takeaway: EC2 instances scale with EC2 Auto Scaling; ECS tasks and DynamoDB capacity scale with Application Auto Scaling.
items.twin: If the stem said "a fleet of EC2 instances" instead: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, because for instances you [use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](../facts/aws-auto-scaling.md#aws-auto-scaling-wa-ec2-auto-scaling-for-instances-application-auto-scaling-for-other-services).
items.say: ECS tasks and DynamoDB capacity aren't EC2, so I'd use Application Auto Scaling for both.

solvers.stem_only: Application Auto Scaling, with target tracking policies for the ECS service desired count and for the DynamoDB table read and write capacity.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The security team has built a new, patched AMI. Every running instance must be replaced with an instance from the new AMI, and at least 90% of the desired capacity must stay in service during the change. The company follows an immutable infrastructure model and does not patch instances in place. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Every running instance must be replaced
at least 90% of the desired capacity

options.text: Create a launch template version with the new AMI, make it the version that the group uses, and wait for the group to update the running instances.
options.why: A new version changes later launches only: running instances stay, and new or replacement instances use the [current settings of the Auto Scaling group](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-replacement-uses-current-settings).

options.text: Edit the launch configuration of the group so that it names the new AMI, and let the group apply the edit to the running instances.
options.why: You [can't modify a launch configuration](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-config-immutable) after you create it, so the edit in this option is not possible.

options.text: Create a launch template version with the new AMI, make it the version that the group uses, and start an instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage of 90%.
options.why: The refresh replaces every running instance with one from the new version and keeps 90% of the desired capacity in service while it works.

options.text: Create a launch template version with the new AMI, make it the version that the group uses, and terminate the old instances by hand, a few at a time.
options.why: It works, but someone terminates and watches each batch by hand, while an instance refresh does the same work as one managed operation.

items.explanation: An instance refresh is the managed way to replace running instances, for example when [deploying a new Amazon Machine Image (AMI)](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-instance-refresh-use-cases). Its minimum healthy percentage is the share of [the desired capacity to keep in service](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-instance-refresh-min-max-healthy), so a value of 90% matches the stem. Each instance is replaced, not patched, which keeps the model immutable.
items.takeaway: A new launch template version changes future launches; an instance refresh replaces the instances that already run.
items.twin: If the stem said "all instances can be replaced at the same time" instead: an instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage of [0 percent](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-instance-refresh-all-at-once).
items.say: I'd add a template version with the new AMI and start an instance refresh.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: every running instance moves to the new AMI, at least 90% of the capacity stays in service, and nothing is patched in place, because the model is immutable.
Before I look at the options, I predict a new launch template version plus an instance refresh, because a new version alone changes only the instances that launch later.

I remove the edit of the launch configuration, because a launch configuration cannot be modified after it is created. I remove the option that only waits, because the running instances keep their old AMI.

Between the instance refresh and terminating the old instances by hand the difference is who does the work; the stem says LEAST operational overhead, so the managed refresh wins, and its minimum healthy percentage keeps 90% in service.
Check: the instance refresh replaces every instance, keeps 90% of the capacity in service and changes nothing in place. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: New launch template version with the patched AMI, set it on the group, start an instance refresh with minimum healthy percentage 90.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The load balancer is enabled in Availability Zone A and Availability Zone B. The Auto Scaling group has one subnet, in Availability Zone A, so every instance runs in that zone. The company needs the web tier to be highly available across multiple Availability Zones. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: enabled in Availability Zone A and Availability Zone B
has one subnet, in Availability Zone A

options.text: Add a subnet in Availability Zone B to the Auto Scaling group, so that the group places its instances in both zones.
options.why: The [desired capacity is distributed across these Availability Zones](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-desired-spread-across-azs), and the load balancer already sends traffic to zone B.

options.text: Add a subnet in Availability Zone C to the Auto Scaling group, and keep the load balancer enabled in zones A and B.
options.why: The load balancer is not enabled in zone C, and for registered targets in such a zone it [does not route traffic to them](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lb-no-traffic-to-disabled-az).

options.text: Extend the Auto Scaling group into a second AWS Region, and register the new instances with the same load balancer.
options.why: Auto Scaling groups are Regional: they [can span Availability Zones, but not AWS regions](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-regional-spans-azs-not-regions).

options.text: Create a second Auto Scaling group with a subnet in Availability Zone B, and attach it to the same target group.
options.why: It works, but two groups mean two sets of scaling policies and settings to keep in step, and one group can use both zones.

items.explanation: Instances in one zone share that zone's fate: if it fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances). AWS recommends a group [across multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-resilience-practices) with the load balancer in the same zones. Zone B is already enabled on the load balancer, so one more subnet in the group completes the design.
items.takeaway: For high availability, give one Auto Scaling group subnets in several zones that the load balancer also uses.
items.twin: If the stem said "keep running if the whole Region fails" instead: a second group in another Region, because groups are [regional constructs](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-regional-spans-azs-not-regions).
items.say: Add a zone B subnet to the group; the load balancer already serves zone B.

solvers.stem_only: Add a subnet in AZ B (where the ALB is already enabled) to the Auto Scaling group so it balances instances across both zones.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. When the group launches an instance, a user data script downloads configuration files for several minutes. The load balancer sends requests to new instances before the script finishes, and users see errors. The company must ensure that no new instance receives traffic before its script ends, and the solution must work automatically for every new instance. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: no new instance receives traffic before its script ends

options.text: Increase the health check grace period of the Auto Scaling group so that it covers the minutes that the user data script needs.
options.why: The grace period is the [minimum amount of time (in seconds)](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-grace-period-definition) before the group can terminate a new unhealthy instance; it does not delay registration.

options.text: Turn on slow start for the target group so that each new instance receives a small share of the requests while the script runs.
options.why: Slow start still sends requests to the new instance, a smaller share at first, so some users still see errors.
options.misconception: believes that slow start keeps requests away from an instance that is not ready

options.text: Detach the target group from the Auto Scaling group, and use an AWS Lambda function to register each instance after its script reports success.
options.why: It works, but the team writes and runs custom registration code for a pause that a lifecycle hook gives as a group feature.

options.text: Add a launch lifecycle hook to the Auto Scaling group, and make the user data script call CompleteLifecycleAction after the files are in place.
options.why: The script ends the wait itself: you [add the CompleteLifecycleAction API call](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-user-data-complete) to user data, and then the group registers the instance.

items.explanation: The group [registers your instance with the load balancer](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-registers-with-lb-before-inservice) as the last step before InService. A launch hook holds the new instance in [Pending:Wait](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-launch-hook-states) before that step, so registration waits until the script reports that the application is [ready to accept traffic](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-lb-registration).
items.takeaway: To keep traffic away until setup ends, use a launch lifecycle hook, not the health check grace period.
items.twin: If the stem said "logs must be copied to Amazon S3 before scale in removes an instance" instead: a termination lifecycle hook, which [pauses the instance before it is terminated](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-scale-in-use).
items.say: A launch lifecycle hook holds the instance until the script finishes, so it gets no traffic early.

solvers.stem_only: Use a launch lifecycle hook: the instance waits in Pending:Wait, not registered with the target group, and the user data script calls CompleteLifecycleAction when done.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The application keeps user session data in the memory of each instance. When the group scales in, the users on the terminated instances are signed out. The company needs a scalable, stateless web tier that keeps scaling in and out without signing users out. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: session data in the memory of each instance

options.text: Configure the Auto Scaling group to copy the session data of the running instances to every new instance when it launches.
options.why: [Data is not automatically copied](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-data-not-copied-to-new-instances) to new instances, and a copy at launch does not save the sessions of the instance that terminates.

options.text: Change the application to store the session data in an Amazon DynamoDB table that every instance in the group reads and writes.
options.why: A DynamoDB table is a managed store that every instance reads, so the group can remove any instance and the user stays signed in.

options.text: Turn on sticky sessions for the target group so that each user returns to the instance that holds the user's session data.
options.why: Sticky sessions [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what), but the session still lives on that instance and is lost at scale in.

options.text: Change the application to store the session data in a cache that the team installs and runs on a separate group of EC2 instances.
options.why: It works, but the team patches, scales and repairs its own cache instances, which is more operational work than a managed table.

items.explanation: Session data in the memory of an instance goes away with the instance. Well-Architected says to offload session data to a [database, cache, or external files](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-offload-session-data), and data that must survive scale in is [stored off the instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-persist-data-off-instance). Then [they can scale horizontally](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-stateless-scales-horizontally): any instance can serve any request.
items.takeaway: A stateless tier keeps session data off the instance, so the group can remove any instance.
items.twin: If the stem said "keeps uploaded files on the local disk of each instance" instead: Amazon S3, because data that must survive scale in is [stored off the instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-persist-data-off-instance).
items.say: I'd move the sessions to DynamoDB, so any instance can serve any user.

solvers.stem_only: Externalize session state to a managed shared store (ElastiCache or DynamoDB) so any instance can serve any user.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. A new instance needs several minutes to start before it can serve requests. Traffic follows a predictable pattern: it rises to a peak from 09:00 to 11:00 every weekday. Users must not see slow responses during a rise in traffic that can be anticipated. A few minutes of slow responses are acceptable during a rise that cannot be anticipated. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.text: Add a target tracking scaling policy that keeps the average CPU utilization of the group near a target value, with no scheduled actions.
options.why: Target tracking is dynamic scaling, [which is reactive in nature](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-long-initialization-fit): the instances start minutes after the 09:00 rise, and users see slow responses.
options.misconception: expects a metric-based policy to add capacity before a known peak arrives

options.text: Add scheduled actions that raise the minimum capacity before 09:00 and lower it after 11:00 on weekdays, and add a target tracking scaling policy.
options.why: You can [use scheduled scaling and scaling policies together](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-plus-policies-together): the raised minimum is in place before the peak, and target tracking removes capacity after 11:00.

options.text: Add a predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode that adds and removes instances from its forecast, with no other scaling policy.
options.why: Predictive scaling launches early, but [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in), so a policy that removes instances from its forecast does not exist.

options.text: Set the minimum, maximum and desired capacity of the group to the number of instances that the highest daily peak needs.
options.why: It works, but the group pays for the peak capacity outside 09:00 to 11:00 as well, which costs more than scheduled actions.

items.explanation: The peak is known, and a new instance needs minutes to start, so the capacity is needed before 09:00. Scheduled scaling fits when [the need arises on a predictable schedule](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use). A scheduled action sets [desired, minimum, and maximum capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-action-sets-capacities) at a set time, and target tracking then follows the load inside those limits.
items.takeaway: A known peak and slow-starting instances: raise capacity with a scheduled action, and let target tracking follow the rest.
items.twin: If the stem said "Traffic rises to a peak several times a day at unpredictable times, with no daily or weekly pattern" instead: target tracking alone, because dynamic scaling fits when [you don't know when the traffic will change](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use).
items.say: The peak is on a schedule, so I'd raise the minimum before nine and let target tracking handle the rest.

solvers.stem_only: Scheduled actions to raise capacity before the known 09:00-11:00 weekday peak and lower it after, plus a target tracking policy for unexpected rises (predictive plus target tracking would also fit).

items.stem: A company uses an Amazon SQS queue to decouple its web tier from an image-processing tier. Worker instances in an Auto Scaling group poll the queue. One worker needs about 2 seconds to process one message, and each message must be processed within 60 seconds after it arrives. The number of uploaded images changes a lot during the day, so the processing tier must be scalable. Which scaling configuration will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: about 2 seconds to process one message

options.text: A target tracking scaling policy on the ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric of the queue, with a target value of 30 messages
options.why: The queue length [might not change proportionally](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-queue-length-not-proportional) to the size of the group, so the policy adds the wrong number of workers.

options.text: A target tracking scaling policy on the average CPU utilization of the worker group, with a target value of 50 percent
options.why: For queue work, AWS says [100% CPU utilization is expected and should not be your primary metric](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-queue-depth-metric-for-batch-work); the queue shows the waiting work.
options.misconception: treats CPU utilization as the measure of queued work

options.text: A fixed group size that matches the number of workers needed at the highest daily upload rate, with no scaling policy
options.why: It works, but the group pays for peak workers all day; when uploads change, AWS says [you might consider using dynamic scaling](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-dynamic-scaling-when-load-varies).

options.text: A target tracking scaling policy on metric math that divides ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible by GroupInServiceInstances, with a target value of 30
options.why: The metric falls as workers are added, so target tracking adds workers when the backlog grows and removes them when it shrinks.

items.explanation: One worker clears a message in 2 seconds, and a message can wait 60 seconds, so one worker can hold a backlog of 30. AWS says to take the acceptable latency and [divide it by the average time](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-acceptable-backlog-per-instance-target) per message. The metric is the [backlog per instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance): [ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance-metric-math) divided by GroupInServiceInstances, which metric math calculates.
items.takeaway: Scale queue workers on backlog per instance; the target is the acceptable latency divided by the time per message.
items.twin: If the stem said "about 6 seconds to process one message" instead: the same metric with a target of 10, because you take the latency and [divide it by the average time](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-acceptable-backlog-per-instance-target).
items.say: I'd scale the workers on backlog per instance, with a target of thirty messages per worker.

solvers.stem_only: Target tracking on backlog per instance (ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible divided by in-service instances) with acceptable backlog 60 s / 2 s = 30.

items.stem: A company runs stateless video-encoding workers on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The workers take jobs from a queue, and the jobs can tolerate interruption and can be restarted, but each restart delays a job, so Spot interruptions must stay rare. At least two workers must keep running even if Amazon EC2 reclaims Spot capacity. The number of other workers changes with the number of jobs. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: At least two workers must keep running

options.text: Use a mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base capacity of 2 instances, and use Spot Instances for all capacity above the base.
options.why: Anything above the base can run on Spot, or on a [specified percentage mix of On-Demand or Spot instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-on-demand-base-spot-above); here the mix is all Spot.

options.text: Run every worker as an On-Demand Instance, and scale the group with a target tracking policy on the backlog per instance.
options.why: It works, but Spot Instances cost [up to 90%](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-discount-up-to-90-percent) less than On-Demand prices, and these jobs can be restarted.

options.text: Specify one instance type in the mixed instances policy, and use the lowest-price allocation strategy for the Spot Instances.
options.why: The lowest-price strategy has the [highest risk of interruption](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-spot-lowest-price-not-recommended), and one instance type gives Spot fewer pools to choose from.

options.text: Specify several instance types in the mixed instances policy, and use the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy for the Spot Instances.

items.stem: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Traffic follows a predictable daily pattern with a peak every morning; after the peak, the load falls to a level that changes from day to day. The group has one predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode and no other scaling policy. The instances are ready before each morning peak, but the group keeps its peak capacity for the rest of the day and through the night, and the monthly cost has grown. The application must stay ready for the morning peak. Which change will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: keeps its peak capacity for the rest of the day

options.text: Switch the predictive scaling policy to forecast only mode, so that the policy removes the extra instances when the forecast falls.
options.why: In [forecast only](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-forecast-only-mode-first) mode the policy forecasts capacity but does not scale the group, so it removes nothing and also stops the morning scale-out.

options.text: Add a scheduled action each evening that sets the desired capacity to the night level, and keep the predictive scaling policy.
options.why: It works, but capacity stays at the peak level until the evening, and a fixed night level stays the same while the load changes each day.

options.text: Add a target tracking scaling policy on average CPU utilization, and keep the predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode.
options.why: Target tracking removes instances when the metric falls below the target, and the predictive policy keeps [launching capacity in advance of forecasted load](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-long-initialization-fit).

options.text: Let predictive scaling raise and lower the maximum capacity of the group automatically when the forecast changes.
options.why: A maximum that predictive scaling raised [does not automatically decrease back](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-raised-max-stays) to the original value, so this setting cannot lower it.
options.misconception: believes that predictive scaling lowers the maximum capacity again after it raised it

items.explanation: Predictive scaling adds instances ahead of the forecast, but [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in). You can [combine predictive scaling and dynamic scaling](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-combine-policy-types-predictive-plus-dynamic): the predictive policy keeps the mornings ready, and the target tracking policy removes instances when the load falls.
items.takeaway: Pair predictive scaling with target tracking: predictive scaling adds capacity early, but [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in).
items.twin: If the stem said "traffic has no daily or weekly pattern" instead: target tracking without the predictive policy, because dynamic scaling fits when [you don't know when the traffic will change](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use).
items.say: Predictive scaling only scales out, so I'd add target tracking to bring capacity down at night.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the change that is MOST cost-effective.
I mark the constraints: one predictive policy in forecast and scale mode, the mornings must stay ready, and capacity stays at the peak level for the rest of the day and through the night.
Before I look at the options, I predict forecast only mode, because I think that mode lets the forecast remove the extra instances at night.
I remove the option that raises and lowers the maximum automatically, because a maximum that predictive scaling raised does not go back down automatically.

Between forecast only mode and a target tracking policy the difference is what scales in. My first idea breaks because forecast only mode does not scale the group at all, in either direction, and predictive scaling does not scale in. So the group needs a dynamic policy, and target tracking follows the load, which costs less than a fixed evening action.
Check: target tracking plus the predictive policy keeps the mornings ready and removes capacity at night. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Predictive scaling scales out ahead of the forecast but does not scale in on its own; add a dynamic policy (target tracking) next to it so the group removes instances as the load falls, and keep predictive scaling for the morning peak.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The Region has three Availability Zones. At peak load, the application needs 6 instances. The application must be fault tolerant across multiple Availability Zones: if one zone fails, 6 instances must keep serving requests with no wait for new instances. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: with no wait for new instances

options.text: Keep the minimum capacity at 6 instances, and rely on the group to launch replacement instances in the other zones after a zone fails.
options.why: Replacements arrive [within minutes](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-replacement-time-minutes), so users wait for capacity; that is high availability, not the fault tolerance that the stem asks for.

options.text: Configure the Auto Scaling group and the load balancer to use subnets in three Availability Zones of the Region.
options.why: AWS recommends a group [across multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-resilience-practices) with the load balancer in the same zones; three zones keep the spare share small.

options.text: Configure the group to use two Availability Zones, and set the minimum capacity to 12 instances, with 6 in each zone.
options.why: It works, but two zones need six instances each, twelve in all, which costs more than nine instances across three zones.

options.text: Set the minimum capacity of the group to 9 instances, so that each of the three Availability Zones runs 3 instances.
options.why: Nine instances in three zones leave six when one zone fails, so the peak load is served with no launch and no wait.

options.text: Extend the Auto Scaling group into a second AWS Region, and keep 6 instances in each Region behind the same load balancer.
options.why: An Auto Scaling group [can span Availability Zones, but not AWS regions](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-regional-spans-azs-not-regions), so one group cannot extend into a second Region.

items.explanation: Fault tolerant here means no wait after a zone fails, so the spare capacity runs before the failure. Well-Architected says [static stability is preferred for high availability](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-static-stability-for-az-loss) when a whole zone is lost. Three zones with three instances each still leave six after one zone fails, with the fewest instances.
items.takeaway: Fault tolerant across zones: size the group so that the remaining zones carry the peak without new launches.
items.twin: If the stem said "a short wait for new instances is acceptable" instead: six instances across the zones, because the group can [launch instances in another one to compensate](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-az-unavailable-launch-elsewhere).
items.say: Three zones with three instances each, so losing a zone still leaves six running.

solvers.stem_only: Use three AZs with 3 instances each (minimum 9): losing one zone leaves 6, which is cheaper than 6 per zone in two zones (12).

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. A new instance needs several minutes to start before it can serve requests. Traffic rises to a peak several times a day at unpredictable times, with no daily or weekly pattern. Users must not see slow responses during a rise in traffic that can be anticipated. A few minutes of slow responses are acceptable during a rise that cannot be anticipated. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: A few minutes of slow responses are acceptable

options.text: Add a target tracking scaling policy that keeps the average CPU utilization of the group near a target value, with no scheduled actions.
options.why: It adds instances when the metric rises and removes them afterwards, [scaling in more gradually when traffic is decreasing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-target-tracking-scale-in-gradual), so idle capacity stays small.

options.text: Add scheduled actions that raise the minimum capacity before 09:00 and lower it after 11:00 on weekdays, and add a target tracking scaling policy.
options.why: It works, but the raised weekday minimum pays for extra instances that the stem gives no reason for, because the peaks follow no schedule.

options.text: Add a predictive scaling policy in forecast and scale mode that adds and removes instances from its forecast, with no other scaling policy.
options.why: [Predictive scaling uses patterns to scale out](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-predictive-patterns-vs-scheduled-times), and [it will not scale in to remove capacity](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-does-not-scale-in), so it fits neither this traffic nor the claim in the option.

options.text: Set the minimum, maximum and desired capacity of the group to the number of instances that the highest daily peak needs.
options.why: It works, but the group runs the peak number of instances all day, although the stem accepts a few minutes of slow responses.

items.explanation: The peaks have no pattern, so no setting can add instances before them, and the stem accepts a few minutes of slow responses. Target tracking [adjusts the number of EC2 instances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-target-tracking-definition) to hold a target, so it follows each peak up and down. Dynamic scaling fits when [you don't know when the traffic will change](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-vs-dynamic-when-to-use).
items.takeaway: Peaks at unknown times: use target tracking, which reacts to the load and scales in after it.
items.twin: If the stem said "Traffic follows a predictable pattern: it rises to a peak from 09:00 to 11:00 every weekday" instead: scheduled actions plus target tracking, because you can [use scheduled scaling and scaling policies together](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-plus-policies-together).
items.say: There's no pattern to plan for, so target tracking alone is the cheapest fit.

solvers.stem_only: No pattern to schedule or forecast, so only a dynamic target tracking policy; a few minutes of lag is accepted.

items.stem: A company runs an API on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The group is attached to a target group of an Application Load Balancer and keeps its default health check settings. After some days of running, a memory leak makes the API on some instances return HTTP 503 errors. The target group marks these instances as unhealthy, but they stay in the group, and the other instances become overloaded. The company must ensure that such instances are replaced automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: keeps its default health check settings
The target group marks these instances as unhealthy, but they stay in the group

options.text: Configure the target group to terminate each instance that fails its health checks, so that the Auto Scaling group launches a new instance in its place.
options.why: A failed check makes the load balancer [stop routing requests to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-elb-requests-before-detection-fail); replacing the instance is work for the group.

options.text: Turn on Amazon EBS health checks for the Auto Scaling group, so that the group also replaces each instance whose API returns HTTP 503 errors.
options.why: EBS health checks test whether volumes are reachable and [passing I/O status checks](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-ebs-check-must-be-turned-on); a leaking API on a healthy volume passes them.
options.misconception: believes that EBS health checks test the application on the instance

options.text: Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group, so that the group also acts on the health that the load balancer reports.
options.why: With this setting, [Elastic Load Balancing stops sending traffic to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace) and [Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling replaces the unhealthy instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace), with no code to run.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the unhealthy host count of the target group that invokes an AWS Lambda function to mark each failing instance unhealthy.
options.why: It works through [SetInstanceHealth](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-set-instance-health-custom-check), but an alarm and a function are more to build and run than one group setting.

items.explanation: The API fails while each instance keeps running, so the EC2 status checks still pass. By default the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks, so unhealthy targets stay in it. For the ELB health check type, [you must turn it on](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-check-must-be-turned-on); then the group marks such an instance unhealthy [on its next periodic health check](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-unhealthy-replaced) and replaces it.
items.takeaway: When the load balancer sees a failure that the EC2 checks miss, turn on the ELB health check type.
items.twin: If the stem said "the group has no load balancer, and the worker process crashes" instead: a custom health check, because the group [only replaces instances that are unhealthy or unreachable](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lb-default-ec2-checks-only) by the EC2 checks.
items.say: The group ignores the load balancer checks until you turn them on, so I'd turn on ELB health checks.

solvers.stem_only: The group uses only EC2 status checks by default, so it ignores the target group's verdict. Turn on the ELB health check type for the Auto Scaling group so instances the load balancer marks unhealthy are replaced automatically; no custom code needed.
